title: The Outbreak Detective
principle: Studying who gets ill and why is called epidemiology.

t: In 1854 a doctor stopped a cholera outbreak by drawing a map. He never found the germ.

John Snow ended a cholera outbreak in Soho in 1854 without knowing what caused cholera, without a microscope, and without any theory that would be recognised as correct today. He drew a map of the deaths.
sub: He did not need to know what it was. He needed to know where it came from.
That gap — between identifying a cause and stopping a disease — is the whole of this lesson.

question: What would you plot to find the source of an outbreak?
What is the first thing to map in an outbreak investigation?
options: Where every case is, and what they all had in common
stages.outcome: Where every case is, and what they all had in common
note: Commit. Note that Snow's decisive evidence was not the cluster but the exceptions to it.

t: Investigate the outbreak. Any part fits any slot, so the marking is on you.
Assemble the investigation. Placement is unconstrained, then it is tested — and one step is the one that actually convinced people.

parts.label: Define what counts as a case

label: Decide who you are counting, before you count
Find the thing every case did
Account for the people who should have been ill and were not
Stop it, without waiting to be certain

name: Count the right people
Case definition
pass: Everyone is counting the same thing.
A consistent case definition makes the counts comparable.
fail: Different people counted different things, and the pattern is noise.
Without a case definition the data cannot be pooled or compared, and any cluster you find may be an artefact of who was counting.

name: See the pattern
Mapping
pass: The cases cluster around one point.
Spatial clustering is visible and points somewhere.
fail: A list of cases with no pattern anyone can see.
A table of addresses hides what a map shows immediately. The representation is not cosmetic.

name: Find the shared exposure
Common factor
pass: They all drew water from the same pump.
A common exposure is identified across cases.
fail: A cluster, and no idea what the people in it had in common.
Clustering alone gives a location, not a cause. Something has to link the cases to a specific exposure.

name: Convince anybody
The exceptions
pass: The brewery workers drank beer and stayed well. The widow who liked that water died miles away.
Negative and distant cases are accounted for, which is what turns a correlation into an argument.
fail: A good story that any sceptic can pick apart.

Snow's strongest evidence was the exceptions: workhouse and brewery residents inside the cluster who were not ill, and a woman who died in Hampstead because she had the water delivered. Explaining what does NOT fit is what made it persuasive.

name: Actually stop it
Action
pass: The pump handle comes off and the outbreak ends.
The exposure is removed while the causal question is still open.
fail: A beautiful analysis and people still dying.
Waiting for certainty costs lives. Snow acted without knowing what cholera was, and was right.

win: You found it, explained the odd cases, and stopped it — without knowing what it was.
All five. Note the fourth: explaining what did not fit is what turned a suggestive map into an argument.
lose: Read which step failed — it names what was in the wrong job.
Each failed trial names the step that was skipped. Reassign and re-test.

t: Studying who gets ill and why is called epidemiology.
Epidemiology studies the distribution of disease in populations. It can identify and remove a cause without any understanding of the mechanism.
This is inference from pattern rather than from mechanism — the same forensic reasoning you met in the evidence lesson, applied to populations.

Snow's map is famous and his best evidence was elsewhere: a natural experiment in which two water companies supplied intermingled houses in south London from different points on the Thames. Households were effectively randomised by which company happened to serve them, and the death rates differed by a factor of about eight. That is a controlled comparison found rather than constructed.
sub: He was wrong about a lot. He was right about the pump.
Snow's underlying theory was incomplete and the germ was not identified for another thirty years. Removing the handle worked anyway.
Which is the useful lesson: you can act correctly on an incomplete understanding, and waiting for a full one costs lives.

It is also a caution in the other direction. Snow was resisted for years, partly because miasma theory explained the same data adequately and partly because his conclusion was inconvenient. Being right early is not the same as being believed early.

q: Did Snow know what caused cholera?
Did Snow's intervention depend on identifying the pathogen?
What does the case show about the relation between mechanism and action?
options: No — but he knew where it was coming from, and that was enough
No, so his intervention did not really work
why: Nobody knew about the germ for another thirty years. He worked out where it was coming from by looking at who got ill, and taking the pump handle off stopped it.
The bacterium was not identified until 1884. Snow's argument was entirely about exposure patterns, and removing the exposure worked without any knowledge of what was being removed.

Mechanism and action are separable. Knowing the cause is sufficient for action and not necessary for it — identifying a removable exposure can be enough. That is why epidemiology functions as an independent discipline rather than an applied branch of microbiology, and why it usually gets there first.

t: Every food poisoning outbreak is still solved this way.

Case definition, map, common exposure, explain the exceptions, remove the source. That sequence identifies a contaminated batch of salad or a restaurant in days, usually before any laboratory has finished typing the organism — and the action does not wait for the laboratory.
